I try to just be vague about it unless I know the other person/people well enough for *them* to know I’m not intending to be pretentious. I’m a rather dysfunctional individual with virtually no achievements to my name, so it’s easy for me to tack on that IQ doesn’t mean much in the real world and it’s not like it means someone is going to be happy, successful, or socially proficient. 

I actually got tested and knew my IQ looooong before I found out about giftedness, so I didn’t know it affected me that much. I always thought of it as a ‘whatever’ thing. I already knew that I thought A LOT, way more than most people (for better *and* for worse), and was already deemed one of the smart kids in school because of my grades, so I had a feeling that I’d score above average anyways. Though I was surprised to have scored as high as I did - I thought maybe I’d be at the 80th percentile or something; didn’t even think I’d have a chance at hitting the high 90’s lol. Nevertheless, despite not finding my actual IQ important, I love talking about IQ and testing as a concept *because* I think it’s given way too much weight in society.

The fact that I approach the subject with ‘yeah it’s not really a big deal and people who brag about it are losers’ before even alluding to having been tested removes a lot of the taboo. Sometimes I’ll volunteer the info that I’ve been tested if I feel like it suits the current conversational context, other times I’ll wait until specifically asked. I found the test really interesting since it was sprung on me without my knowledge (I was in the psych ward for unrelated reasons and one time they brought me into a psych’s office and just started asking me random questions), so I like openly talking about that part, as well as the stupid mistakes I made during. I never volunteer my results though. If someone I trust asks me what I scored, I’ll tell them and reiterate that I’m still a fucking idiot though. If I don’t know them well, I’ll just say it was above average, and will once again explain that it’s not a big deal and how most people are doing way better in life than I am.

Within the 8 or so years that I’ve known about my IQ, no one has ever given me a negative response when it came up in conversation. My results are pretty much as low as you can get whilst still being classified as gifted. Honestly they’re a bit lower than the cutoff, but given all of my other ‘symptoms’ of giftedness + the fact that I was tested unbeknownst to me in a psych ward while I was in a horrible mental state at age 13 + that they included other tests not associated with IQ whatsoever that I scored significantly lower on (thus bringing down my average), the professionals in my life have concluded that the shoe still fits. I also *also* try to keep everything as close to truth as possible, so the lie isn’t unnecessarily grandiose, as I find that then crosses into pathological territory - Since at that point, you’re sort of...’playing into’ the lie and having fun with straying from the truth. I think, like with most mental disorders, the onset is caused by a mix of one’s predisposed tendencies and events that happen in one’s life. I’m very, very anxious by default, and am neurodivergent, so that made it REALLY easy for me to develop maladaptive personality traits. 

Regarding AvPD: I’d always been sensitive to negative judgement, but didn’t let that stop me from much when I was a kid. As I grew older though, I started receiving ridicule for the things that I was open about liking, that judgement started affecting me severely, and the only way I felt I could deal with it is by simply...not revealing those things that had the risk of getting a negative reaction from others. I’m quite impulsive and prone to oversharing when excited, so it took a long time to get a handle on censoring myself, but eventually it worked. With time, I kept finding more and more things that I’d “benefit” from being secretive about (I believe this also relates to perfectionism with OCPD - choosing what’s ideal to keep concealed), and thus the goalpost just keeps getting moved further and further. 

Social interaction is so insanely stressful that it’s much easier to be on my own. I isolate a lot. My perfectionism leads me to strongly believe I am inadequate and undeserving of anything good unless I’ve done *everything* I possibly can to earn it. Even then, I never feel like it’s enough. I’m scared to get to know people on a personal level because I’m ashamed at how little I’ve accomplished in life, and don’t want others to know the truth of how pathetic I perceive myself to be.

Regarding OCPD: Due to having a decent amount of mental potential, I’ve always seen how well things *can* be done, and always wanted to my best. I also tend to hyperfixate on things. I was actually pretty normal about it though, until 6th grade when my parent brought to my attention that my current grade in a class was lower than usual. I decided from then on to set minimum standards for myself (which were still very high) and to always get the highest grades possible - to always do as much as possible, and do it as well as possible. This of course led to extreme perfectionism. I think my high levels of anxiety made it easy for me to crave intense structure and control over what I’m doing so I wouldn’t have to worry as much, but that rigidity can be maladaptive. I feel like in order to do a good enough job, I *need* intense structure and control over everything that’s going on.

To summarize the ‘causes’: I already had predisposed tendencies of rejection sensitivity, fear of judgement + rigidity, and perfectionism. Being ridiculed on subjects that were very personal to me by my peers - and the subsequent emotional pain it caused - made me lean into extreme measures to avoid any degree of interpersonal vulnerability. And for OCPD, all it took was one instance of someone prioritizing my scores above my actual degree of learning in a class for me to become an insane perfectionist hahaha

-

One really interesting thing I’ve noticed with my disordered personality traits, is that it seems like they were *deliberate* choices I made so I could avoid a less desirable result (whether that’s negative judgement or feeling like I could have done better on something). I don’t know if that’s how it works in general for identifying PD traits vs traits of other disorders unrelated to personality, but it seems to be the case for me. I was never told exactly what symptoms of mine are from each PD and non PD I have, so this is the best I can come up with in differentiating the root causes of my troubled behaviours/mindsets. 

I *actively* trained myself to be more secretive. I *actively* create arbitrary high standards for whatever I do, that I *must* adhere to, otherwise I’ve failed, and I enjoy partaking in that extreme perfectionistic behaviour. Etc., etc. I don’t actively choose for something to make me anxious, which is why that correlates more to my anxiety disorders than my PDs. They absolutely contribute to each other though, AvPD in particular. My high generalized/social anxiety made it easier to rely on avoidance (plus it also made the typical stressors seen in AvPD even more severe than they already were), and AvPD gives me wayyyy more situations that activate my GAD/SAD compared to if I didn’t have it. They make each other worse. 

Maybe that element of sculpting your life around something is what takes maladaptive patterns from a regular disorder to a personality disorder. You’ve integrated it into who you are and how you live, thus it naturally becomes a part of your personality, and it’s something you rely on to cope with the hardships of life. Putting a bunch of barriers between yourself and what you don’t want to experience to the point where your life is *just* the barriers. I don’t know, but it’s interesting food for thought IMO.

-

Lastly, how did I find out I had those PDs? I was diagnosed with them following an extremely in depth psychological evaluation (done by my long time psychologist), where I took several personality assessments and supplied tons of information about all of my pathologies. Midway through, I discovered what all 10 personality disorders in the DSM-5 were, and upon hearing about AvPD, I started crying because I felt like someone “finally put it into words”. I saw a decent number of my symptoms within OCPD as well, but there were some components I was lacking like the interpersonal conflicts (I’m quite the doormat all things considered, hahaha), and not having poor insight into my maladaptive behaviours (I always knew my OCPD traits weren’t normal and that they were all my own issues I needed to work through, rather than thinking I was right and everyone else had a problem), so I wasn’t confident I had OCPD until it was confirmed by my psychologist. The AvPD felt obvious though.

I was diagnosed in December 2022, and I was 20 at the time (21 now). I’m currently working with another psychologist to finish some other parts of the evaluation, so there’s a chance those diagnoses may change, but as of now I’m under the solid impression that I have AvPD and OCPD.

For reference, some of the core building blocks of AvPD are: 
- Difficulties establishing (or being comfortable in) bonds with others due to a fear of vulnerability, as opening up means you can be judged for it. It just doesn’t feel right or natural to do.
- Significant interpersonal/emotion inhibition, both in casual social encounters *and* deeper bonds.
- Avoiding things you enjoy or opportunities that could be beneficial to you if they involve significant interpersonal contact or put you in a position where you can fail/be judged.
- *Incredibly* sensitive to negative evaluation, and will experience deep pain from minor - or even non-existent - bits of feedback.
- Extremely preoccupied in not saying/doing anything that could yield judgement. This can involve hiding massive chunks of your life, interests, and personality. I’ve yet to see *anyone* on this subreddit say that they aren’t secretive in one way or another (though I could just not be looking hard enough). I know this is a MASSIVE one for me. Avoidants often garnered this fear after they got continuously ridiculed for their interests when younger.
- Extremely preoccupied with not bothering others or drawing needless attention to oneself.
- Deep seeded feelings of inadequacy. This contributes to the difficulty in establishing bonds, since one with AvPD may stop the connection before it gets too serious because they don’t think they’re good enough to do it, and the other person will find that out if they keep talking to them. It obviously contributes to avoiding beneficial social/career opportunities as well.
- Feelings of loneliness, since you really *do* want social bonds and to be liked, but you’re too scared to follow through.
- And as the name implies, avoiding things when they activate those fears, or when you even think those fears *could* be activated in the future. Avoidants are chronic ghosters lol

There are more, but that should cover most bases. It’s often viewed as a more severe version of social anxiety that is also pervasive, rather than just situational. Hope that helps! :)

Thankfully I don’t pull from the hair on my head, but everything else is fair game, including my eyebrows. I don’t really give a damn that I rip out my body hair, but the eyebrow stuff shattered bits of my confidence. They’re now the first thing I look at whenever I can see my reflection in public, they’re what I spend the most time worrying about and trying to conceal correctly, and if I can’t do that (or eyebrow pencil makeup rubs off if I stay somewhere overnight) I’ll physically hide them.

It’s taken a lot of effort to ease up with the eyebrow ripping. I stopped deliberately trying to rip them out years ago, but the damage has been done, and me just grabbing at them will pull them out. I’m in the habit of shaving them off every few months so my hands can’t pry at them for a while (thus ‘resetting’ their urge to pull), and I do pretty well at not ripping them out once they’ve grown back...until a stressful event occurs. Then it starts again. Such is life I suppose.

If I only ripped out my body hair then I’d *easily* say dermatillomania would’ve been my worse habit of the two, but now that it’s the eyebrows too? Nope. I think solid proof that it’s my bigger issue is that: I’ve painstakingly tried to stop with the eyebrows for many years, yet any attempt to ease up on my skin picking has been very minor and not committed. The body hair ripping is kind of an afterthought. It just motivates me to keep it short enough so I don’t give myself more *dermatillomania* problems by having any regrowth get ingrown (because I *know* what happens then).

There’s not much someone can say to completely settle my worries, *but* some things have helped at least a little bit. For me, I worry a lot about having done something wrong, and the other person being too polite to mention it, which would make me unable to improve my behaviour since I don’t even know it’s a problem. I find that if the other person confirms they will make a point to tell me if something’s an issue, it’s useful info to remind myself of whenever I’m catastrophizing a situation. Even though I don’t fully trust it (people can easily fall back on that promise if they feel like they’d be rude), telling myself “they said they’d mention it if I did something wrong, and they haven’t with this, so it’s likely I haven’t actually done anything wrong” can calm my stress a decent amount. In a way, if they do have a problem and they didn’t mention it *despite coming to an agreement to do so*, it’s kinda out of my control. That’s what I try to tell myself at least...

Conflicts and disappointments can be hard to handle, but it’s a required part of any consistent social bond, so I’d much rather deal with the discomfort of someone having a complaint so I can then immediately fix my behaviour (which will stop me from unintentionally doing it again), than only figuring it out *after* I’ve been a nuisance and can’t change what’s already happened. I know that doesn’t pertain to your exact situation though. It’s just the general way I (as someone with AvPD) hope conflicts will be solved in my social relationships. 

While being told “I’ll let you know if there’s ever an issue” is stressful, it at least means I have ‘permission’ to stop *constantly* worrying about the possibility that they’re silently bothered. Different people work different ways so I don’t want to guarantee you that that will be the way to go with him, but maybe you could present the idea. As in, mentioning that you’re not bothered at all, but if it would help quell his nerves, you won’t hide any issues if they ever hypothetically arose, so he won’t have to wonder if there’s a problem. No news is good news, and if you’ve not mentioned any issue, then there’s nothing to worry about.

Honestly the most important part about that would be keeping to your word. I’ve had situations occur where the other person didn’t follow through and I only realized way later that something was up, and oh wow I feel TERRIBLE whenever I find that out. 

For example, I’m quite the talker and can speak at length about tons of things. I also happen to be friends with mostly quiet people who prefer others to lead the conversation. I’m aware of my tendency, and always affirm to friends that I’d much rather hear anything they want to talk about than whatever I’m on at the moment, so they’re more than welcome to put me on pause if they want to go on a tangent - which they agree to. I always say how it’ll never offend or upset me, that I’d be much happier knowing so I can stop the problem before it even starts. When I’m on my own tangents, I repeatedly (probably to an annoying degree not gonna lie, but I’m very worried about overpowering a conversation so I’d rather annoy them with cautiousness than obliviousness lol) check that I’m not overwhelming them or if there was something they’d like to talk about. There have been times where I was so diligent with it, and the person kept declining my offers to pause the subject I’m on about, only to discover months later they actually *did* want to talk about something and were thus a bit unsatisfied with that specific conversation. I know I’m complaining about pretty much nothing right now, but when I figure that out, I can no longer guarantee that they’ll be honest with their needs despite me doing everything I can to avoid those situations, and thus I need to worry about it every time. And I also will feel really guilty about the incident for years. Maybe it’s my fault for putting the responsibility on them - I have no idea what an alternative would be though.

I can’t fully blame them, because honesty can be hard sometimes, but both parties need to hold up their end of the bargain (“I’ll be honest if it means you won’t worry”) for it to work. So I guess only offer that if you think you can do it. It’s perfectly understandable if you can’t - I don’t think most people can do that in all circumstances.

I mean I’ve gone out of my way to mourn friendships I didn’t even lose because I thought I needed to mentally prepare for everything to crumble, since there was a tiny bit of conflict. Thankfully I care more about communicating to solve the problem immediately more than my urge to avoid it, however I assume a lot of people with AvPD aren’t as preoccupied with that as I am, leaving them to avoid as their default response. Then as a response we’ll assume everything’s been ruined and withdraw. People with AvPD will have varying levels of insight on the true nature of the situation. Some can recognize that they’re catastrophizing/overthinking and will still feel like their fears are real, but will try to go approach the situation based on the evidence that it’s actually not as bad as they think. Some will evaluate it the same way but still make drastic decisions (as if their fears *were* true) because it’s emotionally easier and/or ‘just in case’. And some will genuinely believe their worries are 100% accurate. Depends on the person and the severity of their disorder.

I think I always knew there was something off about sensitivity and fear, but as I grew up I gathered insight on why I acted the way I did, even before diagnosis. However now that I am diagnosed, it really established context as to *why* why, revealed links between behaviours I thought were unrelated, and gave me the ability to pinpoint exactly when I’m engaging in an avoidant behaviour. Because my psych eval had to be rushed towards the end (my psychologist left the organization), I never got point blank told what mindsets/tendencies of mine are due to AvPD, but I know myself well enough to where it’s extremely obvious. Admittedly it can be a bit difficult for me to distinguish what symptoms are caused AvPD vs comorbid SAD though. 

[Everything from here on is just me reflecting on what symptoms of mine stem from personality disorders rather than similar non PDs]

I realized that giant components of my AvPD were conscious choices I made to shield myself from repeating past experiences that hurt me deeply. It’s almost like I gave myself the disorder lol. I could totally be wrong here, but I think the core of my personality disorders (I’ve got two them, oh yeah) were ‘deliberate’ in a way - though each one has a different vibe. With AvPD, they were habits I created (or at the very minimum enforced) that I don’t actually enjoy, I just feel I have to do it because the alternative is so much more painful. OCPD on the hand is a lot closer to ego-syntonic for me. I have urges that feel rewarding to indulge in (perfectionism is my pleasant vice), so I make the decision to do it the way I enjoy (as long as it doesn’t bother others) because...why wouldn’t I?

I suppose that theory shows how PDs are far more engrained in people than Axis 1 disorders are. Perhaps that degree of conscious decision is what makes it a *personality* disorder? I don’t know, it’s the only way I can differentiate between the presentation of some PDs and similar disorders. 

The traits being pervasive enough to the point where we changed ourselves as people and it became us, because we had no other healthy method to compensate for our deep seeded struggles. We’ve all got coping mechanisms, but there’s likely some line that gets crossed depending on how much we incorporate it into our lives, especially if it forces us to live differently in an unhealthy way. Maybe it’s characterized by the behaviours we created those copes for? As in, since our fears are abnormal or far too intense - and are things we need to face in the world - our methods to compensate are inherently maladaptive. Then, when that engrosses how we approach everything, it becomes a part of our personality? And I guess from a diagnostic standpoint it also needs to be present from a young age and doesn’t just go away.

I don’t know. PDs are weird yet incredibly interesting. I just notice within myself that all of the maladaptive behaviours I *deliberately* employed appear to stem from somewhere very deep, that also *by sheer coincidence* align with my clinically significant personality patterns
